BREAKING: Jensen Huang releases his first public statement since resigning as CEO of Nvidia, $NVDA, and says he is willing to return as CEO.

Jensen Huang specifically says he will return as CEO if the board asks him to.

Full statement:

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

We continue to believe Nvidia’s board should leave the possibility of Huang returning as CEO open.
Jensen Huang has begun the inevitable comeback tour.

It's officially Nvidia's earnings day.

Today's earnings report and call will likely be the most watched earnings event in history.

We are watching two key things:

1. Do executives show any willingness to reinstate Jensen Huang

2. What has CHANGED from a business perspective

As of now, considering the information over the last 48 hours, we believe there is an <20% chance that Jensen returns.

Any indication that the probability is higher would be strongly bullish for the stock.

But, if not, then what has changed for Nvidia? With or without Jensen, this company remains one of the best businesses in the world.

We are looking to see if the company still expects revenue growth of 70%+ in FY2028, as management previously indicated.

We also look for any changes to AI infrastructure spending, demand for Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips, and the company's relationships with its largest customers.

If the fundamental outlook remains intact, then investors must ask: Does Jensen Huang's departure justify the -$750 billion in lost market cap?

We believe the market has already priced in a significant portion of the uncertainty surrounding Jensen's departure.

At the same time, the long-term AI infrastructure investment cycle remains intact, and Nvidia continues to sit at the center of it.

The burden is now on management to demonstrate that the business can continue executing at the same level without Jensen Huang.

More to come after earnings.

Essential expenses are taking up an increasing portion of US household spending:

Healthcare, housing, utilities, gasoline, financial services, and insurance now account for 45.6% of total US consumer expenditures, near the highest proportion on record.

Over the last 4 years, this figure has risen +1.8 percentage points from its lowest level since 2004.

By comparison, these essential expenses represented a record 46.5% in 2010, following the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, between the 1960s and the 1980s, this proportion never exceeded 40%.

In 1959, these categories accounted for less than 30% of total consumer expenditures.

Mandatory spending is eating up a growing portion of US household budgets.

How I trade is simple -- although to each element of "simple" I have many rules (that I follow)

-Buy or sell an adjusted ATR breakout
-Please stops to disallow the market to dig too deeply in my pockets
-Limit risk per trade to 7/10th of 1% of total nominal capital
-Use open orders
-Move protective stops to B/E as soon as reasonable
-Take partial profits if profit of tranche > 50 basis points
-Take profit at targets
-Use 8 DMA to manage trade

US hiring plans are picking up as seasonal demand accelerates:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up +57% YoY and the highest October total since at least 2009.

Technology led with 300,252 announced positions, followed by Transportation at 100,000, and Retail at 13,300.

Year-to-date hiring plans are up +34% YoY, to 655,304 workers.

Meanwhile, seasonal hiring announcements jumped +26% YoY, to 470,400, but remained 29% below the 660,150 recorded in 2024.

Seasonal positions now account for 72% of all hiring plans in 2026 and nearly 60% of the increase from last year.

Seasonal hiring is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: The top 1% of US businesses by AI spending allocated a record $10,199 per employee to AI in October, according to Ramp data.

Since January 2026, this figure has more than tripled.

The top 10% of firms spent a record $801 per employee last month, up +180% since January.

The median firm's average AI spend per employee rose to a record $16, up +164% since January.

In other words, the top 1% is now spending 625 times more per employee as the typical company.

Meanwhile, AI adoption among US businesses on Ramp rose +1.0 percentage point in October, to a record 56.8%, up from 45.5% in January.

Corporate AI spending is accelerating across the board.
